articles.title_orig: Pope Leo returns to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo returns to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.content_orig:
Lee el artículo en español
Riding on horseback to visit the most isolated Andean areas of his community, distributing food amid the Covid-19 pandemic, or wearing rubber boots in the water and mud of floods: this is how many Peruvians remember the man who is now Pope Leo XIV.
Robert Prevost was in the trenches and alongside his people during Peru’s most difficult moments, and many of these memories will likely be front of mind among the public as they welcome the pope on his visit to his adopted homeland on Wednesday.
The pope’s visit to Peru, which will include visits to Lima, Cusco and Chiclayo, is widely seen as a homecoming for a pontiff who is a Peruvian citizen and who knows the country in depth.
A young Prevost first arrived in the South American country as a missionary in 1985. The years that followed shaped his leadership style, which would later lead him to become the successor to the late Pope Francis.
“I think he was heroic in many ways; he risked becoming ill. We lost 11 priests and a bishop emeritus during that time,” Father José Del Rosario recalls of the most difficult days of the pandemic.
Padre Robert, as he is known in Spanish in Peru, traveled more than 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Chiclayo to the Diocese of Callao, a province bordering the capital, Lima, where he served as apostolic administrator.
“He came every two weeks in his little car; he came alone in a simple pickup truck,” explained Del Rosario, parish priest and rector of the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Mount Carmel of La Legua, who worked closely with the then-bishop.
Pope! Amigo! Peruvians remember the young American priest who became pope
Prevost distributed food and everything needed by a population that lived under lockdown for months, while also offering spiritual guidance during the crisis.
“He gave us a lot of hope and cared for our people, a man who was very close to the people … and also very humble,” Del Rosario added.
Peru recorded more than 219,000 deaths , according to Johns Hopkins University figures, and one of the highest coronavirus mortality rates in the world. In Lima, and especially in the regions, terrifying scenes unfolded outside hospitals, with sick people collapsing in the street due to the shortage of oxygen, one of the key tools for treating the virus.
In Chiclayo, Bishop Prevost launched a fundraising campaign to purchase an oxygen plant. Together with Caritas Chiclayo, the bishop appealed to authorities and sectors of civil society and managed to raise more than US$380,000 for not just one but two oxygen plants.
Janinna Sesa, former director of Caritas Chiclayo, worked with the bishop for eight years, including during the pandemic, the flooding caused by the coastal El Niño in 2017, and Cyclone Yaku in 2023.
“We were always on the front lines, especially during disasters like the coastal El Niño phenomenon. He was the person who put on his boots and waded into the water; he helped people. He was very approachable and very kind,” Sesa told CNN.
Before leaving for Rome in 2023, after the late Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, Bishop Prevost also led appeals for aid for the more than 10,000 people affected by flooding caused by Cyclone Yaku in the north of the country.
“I ask you to be generous; I ask you to open your hearts so that we can help one another and move forward, as we have done in other times of crisis,” Prevost said in a video while standing in the water in the district of Illimo, in the Lambayeque region.
The assistance and response led by Prevost in the face of the massive arrival of Venezuelan migrants in 2018 was comprehensive and had a different vision from that of the country’s other regions.
Peru received more than 1.6 million Venezuelans through November 2025, the second-highest number in the region after Colombia. More than 20,000 of them passed through Chiclayo, and more than 3,500 families settled in the region, according to figures from the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking of the Diocese of Chiclayo. Prevost also promoted this commission to assist migrants and combat human trafficking.
First American pope marks July 4 on migrant island with plea for ‘compassion and generosity’
“The migration flow descended upon us, with thousands of migrants out on the streets, sleeping there, and the parishes serving as shelters,” Sesa recalled.
Father Robert was concerned not only with providing food and collecting clothing, blankets, and medicine, but also with building the San Vicente de Paúl village, which took them in at Puerto Etén.
“His simplicity, the peace he conveys, that serenity Monsignor Prevost had when listening to people — I still see it in Pope Leo XIV…. He welcomed us with such warmth, with so much love,” Lisbeth Díaz, a Venezuelan resident of Chiclayo and member of the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking, told CNN.
Prevost prioritized regularizing their legal status so they could work and integrate into society.
Prevost created spaces for dialogue and encouraged many people to raise their voices to denounce abuses during the internal conflict the country experienced beginning in the 1980s and to openly discuss the social reality during the authoritarian regime of the late President Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s.
At the Augustinian mission in Trujillo, the current pontiff and his seminarians traveled through towns and parishes in Andean areas, staging dramatizations that reflected the violence faced by peasants to encourage conversations that would help heal the trauma and pain they had suffered.
Prevost also participated in collecting signatures for the creation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), which investigated the violence between 1980 and 2000 and human rights abuses, particularly in rural Peru. Trujillo and the parishes led by the current pontiff collected the largest number of signatures.
Leo XIV is a pope forged in Peru. The nearly two decades he spent in the land he adopted as his own profoundly shaped his ministry and set him on the path to the papacy. As a bishop, Prevost was a pastor close to his flock, and at the Vatican, one of his closest collaborators is the Reverend Edgard Rimaycuna, a native of Chiclayo.
His work in South America and his leadership of the Order of Saint Augustine caught the attention of Pope Francis, who first appointed him bishop of Chiclayo and later brought him to Rome, where he went on to hold one of the most important positions in the Vatican and also became a cardinal. This made him a candidate in the 2025 conclave.
Pope Leo presides at biggest Mass of his papacy in Buenos Aires, drawing 2.5 million crowd
In the past, the election of an American pope was considered impossible, given that the College of Cardinals did not wish to associate the papacy with the dominant political and cultural power. However, the cardinals who voted for Cardinal Robert Prevost in the 2025 conclave did not see him simply as a candidate from the United States.
His experience in Peru garnered broad consensus among the cardinals, who chose a bishop with roots in Latin America — someone who speaks Spanish fluently and is attuned to the concerns of the people of that continent.
The pope’s visit to Peru will be an opportunity for the Peruvian people to welcome Padre Robert back to the adopted country that shaped him — and that he shaped deeply as well.
Reverend John Lydon, a priest and member of the same Augustinian religious order to which the pope belongs, and who lived and worked with Prevost for a decade, told CNN: “I believe his dedication to the poor and his defense of human rights will continue to define his visit.”

articles.title_orig: As higher prices seep into broader economy, Fed officials consider faster hikes
articles.title_zh: As higher prices seep into broader economy, Fed officials consider faster hikes
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — More evidence this week of hot inflation in the U.S. was unpleasant news for the Federal Reserve, not to mention consumers: Rising prices may be spreading beyond the one-time shocks from tariffs and high gas prices into the wider economy, meaning that mortgages, credit cards and other forms of borrowing are likely to become increasingly expensive.
Tuesday's consumer price index report showed broadly rising costs across a range of goods and services, some with little connection to more expensive oil and gas or surging investment in artificial intelligence data centers, another factor blamed for worsening inflation. And there is increasing anxiety among Fed officials that higher oil prices stemming from the Iran war may last longer than previously thought.
A key issue debated by Fed policymakers for months has been whether inflation would cool on its own if the Iran war ended and oil prices fell and as the impact of tariffs faded. But government data suggested inflation rose to 4% in October compared with a year ago, up from 3.7% in September, even as gas prices leveled off.
The potential consequences of the new inflation data emerged immediately. Two Fed officials suggested Tuesday that the central bank may have to hike its key interest rate more quickly to tame inflation. Bigger or faster hikes by the Fed would mean that buying a house or a car, or paying off a credit card would become a steeper hill to climb, with millions of Americans already struggling to make ends meet.
Lorie Logan, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas and a voting member of the Fed's rate-setting committee, said Tuesday that price increases remain high for services such as "visits to the doctor, childcare, dining out and hotel stays."
"Prices for these services aren't particularly sensitive to tariffs, conflict in the Middle East or surging demand for computer chips," she added. "While I expect inflation to moderate as price pressures dissipate in energy and manufactured goods, the broader inflationary trend is more likely to persist."
Logan said Tuesday she supported two additional quarter-point rate hikes. While she has made similar statements before, Logan added that the Fed could "move more rapidly this winter" than it "has moved so far this fall," signaling that she may support two rate hikes in a row, a quicker pace than the Fed's current approach.
At its last meeting in late October, the central bank kept rates unchanged at about 3.9%. Chairman Kevin Warsh declined to suggest whether more increases were likely. The central bank hiked rates at its September meeting.
Wall Street investors now see 90% odds that the Fed will lift borrowing costs at its next meeting Dec. 8-9, according to futures prices tracked by CME Fedwatch . Expectations for a second hike at its January meeting tripled between Monday and Tuesday, to more than 64%.
Some Fed officials had expressed optimism over the summer that once the shocks from tariffs and high gas prices faded, inflation would retreat without Fed intervention.
But Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed, poured cold water on that view in a speech late Tuesday.
"Underlying inflation is above target, and it hasn't come down," she said. "That tells me that elevated inflation isn't just about factors that will go away on their own." Still, she also said she supported only gradual rate increases.
Tuesday's inflation report showed prices rising in many areas with little connection to energy costs or AI, including streaming video services, beef and auto insurance.
But surging investment in data centers has driven up the cost of computer chips, power generation equipment, and copper, among other components, with little sign of easing. Prices for smartphones jumped 1.4% just from September to October, the government said, the largest such increase on record.
Computer prices leapt 0.5% last month, and television prices rose 3.3%, reversing the more typical trend in which those prices fall with technological innovation.
The Fed's focus on inflation's spread isn't entirely new. In late August, Chairman Kevin Warsh called attention to data showing that most goods and services were experiencing notable price increases. His speech at the Fed's Jackson Hole symposium signaled that the central bank would hike rates for the first time in three years the following month.
There has been little improvement in inflationary trends since then. On Tuesday, even before October's inflation figures were released, Fed governor Christopher Waller noted in a speech in London that 70% of services prices rose by 3% or more in September from a year earlier.
Waller also said that if monthly core inflation — which excludes food and energy prices — were to reach 0.3% or higher in October, the Fed should consider a half-point interest rate increase next month, double the size of the usual hike.
As it turned out, that's exactly how much core inflation increased.
Even as oil prices have fallen steadily since the beginning of the month as President Donald Trump has suggested fighting could end in the Middle East, Waller noted that energy costs in the U.S. could remain high.
The cost of insuring oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz and taking other steps to avoid attacks has added as much as $20 to $30 a barrel to oil prices, Waller said. Diesel fuel prices will also likely stay high because of a lack of refining capacity, some of which has been destroyed in the Ukraine war, he added.
And while the price of a barrel of oil has slid more than 5% over the last 30 days, it still costs about $30 more than it did at this time last year.
In a Tuesday speech at the Council on Foreign Relations, Fed governor Michelle Bowman suggested that inflation may be getting worse, saying that, "price pressures had been concentrated in a few categories, but the latest data suggest that these pressures may be broadening."

articles.title_orig: Crude Futures Pick Up After Heavy Selling
articles.title_zh: Crude Futures Pick Up After Heavy Selling
articles.content_orig:
This was supposed to be the week that America dramatically escalated its war with Iran.
President Donald Trump repeatedly hinted that US and Israeli attacks on Iran would resume once the midterm elections were over. In anticipation of a military escalation, oil prices spent every single day of October above $100 a barrel, gradually rising to a four-year high of $114 on the last trading day of the month.
Then, a sudden shift: Trump just before the midterms argued that renewed attacks were no longer necessary. And, last Tuesday, Americans voted overwhelmingly for Democrats in a sweeping rebuke of Trump’s Iran policy – a signal that Congress may put up some resistance to the war.
Oil prices plunged over the past week, sinking by $25 to their lowest point in three months and briefly falling below $90 a barrel Tuesday.
Are those events related? Undoubtedly. But the simple political explanation for such a dramatic decline in oil prices fails to account for the astonishing changes happening under the oil market’s hood: Despite the biggest oil supply shock in history, the world is suddenly producing more crude than it consumes.
The oil market has returned to its fundamentals, and they’re looking surprisingly strong.
The story of the oil market throughout the Iran war has been one of remarkable creativity.
Many oil analysts anticipated doomsday scenarios of oil quickly topping $200 a barrel when Iran blocked off tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz pinch point. Instead, oil never came close to hitting the all-time high set in 2008 – or even the more recent peak set in 2022 at the outset of the Russia-Ukraine war.
The market’s resourcefulness – rerouting oil via pipelines and forcing crude tankers through the strait via complex shuttle and military operations – paid off. During occasional days over the past couple months, oil flows through the Middle East have surpassed pre-war averages.
Middle Eastern oil transits certainly haven’t returned to normal. The flows have been volatile, and they were averaging 70% of the pre-war average over the past week, according to oil data tracker Kpler .
But after plunging to 9.8 million barrels per day at the outset of the war in March, oil transits averaged 20.7 million barrels per day last week, according to Natasha Kaneva, head of global commodities research at JPMorgan. That’s closing in on the 24.7 million barrels the Middle East was shipping each day before the war.
(Math time: 20.7 million – 24.7 million = -4 million. Keep that in the back of your head.)
To compensate, oil majors increased output from around the world – particularly from Latin America. Crude flows from outside the Middle East grew by 1.5 million barrels per day from the same point last year.
( More math: -4 million+ 1.5 million = -2.5 million. Keep reading.)
Those increases have been gradual but steady (unlike the topsy turvy Middle East), and energy companies continue to see promise there: Exxon announced Tuesday it has taken preliminary steps that could eventually lead it to return to Venezuela after a two-decade hiatus.
But we’re still at -2.5 million barrels per day. The increase in global production and brute force through the Middle East don’t fully account for how the oil market could return to balance.
The missing element: plunging demand.
Oil consumption has fallen by 3.3 million barrels per day on average during the course of the war, according to JPMorgan, and demand has grown considerably worse over the past couple months. Consumption fell by 3.8 million barrels per day in September and October.
(Last math: -2.5 million + 3.8 million = 1.3 million barrels per day. … OK with rounding it’s actually 1.4 million, but whatever.)
So that’s how you get to an October oil surplus: Stop using as much oil.
The decline in oil demand was in part because high prices forced consumers around the world to make some painful decisions about their energy usage. But fuel prices factored in less to the oil surplus than you might think.
Yes, diesel hit a record high several weeks ago as Ukraine bombarded Russian refineries with drone strikes – until a Trump-negotiated energy ceasefire led to a multi-week respite. And gas prices are on track for a four-year high in 2026, even as they fell below $4 on Tuesday for the first time in several months.
It’s also true that gasoline demand has been in a yearslong slump; electric vehicles are growing increasingly popular – outside the United States, that is; and fuel economy is improving. Improved mileage has put annual per-capita American gas consumption on pace to fall to a post-pandemic low of 390 gallons this year, down from 440 gallons a decade ago, according to Pavel Molchanov, investment strategy analyst at Raymond James.
But both diesel and gas demand slumped primarily for a less obvious reason: refinery constraints. The world simply doesn’t have sufficient refinery infrastructure to make up for lost output from the Middle East and Russia. Global refineries have been working in overdrive.
The world could produce all the oil it wants, but it simply can’t make it into useful fuels fast enough. So, the refining shortfall has been absorbed by sinking global demand – for gas, diesel and the oil that would otherwise be refined into fuel.
The oil surplus has allowed the US to replenish some of its key inventories – particularly in Cushing, Oklahoma, the pipeline crossroads of America. Cushing stockpiles fell below operational minimums in July and are now at their highest level since May , according to the US Energy Information Administration. That gives the key storage facility some much-needed wiggle room, staving off a potential oil price crisis.
A month or two of oil surplus building could give Trump some leverage to wait Iran out.
The US-led blockade against Iran’s ports is working: Iran has exported zero oil through legitimate channels since August, and the economic embargo has sent Iran’s annual inflation rate surging above 70% over the past year – the country’s highest since World War II.
And a Democratic Congress may be able to hold Trump back a bit, but lawmakers will lack significant power to get out of the Iran war.
Still, the “blue tsunami” showed that Iran maintains leverage , too: Trump has been politically weakened, and the election showed Iran can inflict significant economic damage across the world by maintaining a military presence in the Strait of Hormuz.
“This is not a recipe for a quick, acceptable end to the conflict,” said Dan Pickering, founder and chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners. “This is a recipe for more of the same.”

articles.title_orig: If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]
articles.title_zh: If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]
articles.content_orig:
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement.
But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ?
It’s been a very long time since any smartphone launch has generated quite so much buzz. Apple called it a breakthrough in iPhone design.
iPhone Duo features a breakthrough foldable design that’s beautiful, versatile, and durable, opening up possibilities that feel entirely new yet remarkably familiar […]
“iPhone Duo is the most transformational change to iPhone since the original. With an entirely new design and intuitive experiences, it shows what’s possible when hardware and software are engineered together and redefines what it means to use a foldable phone,” said John Ternus.
Despite not really being the target market for the phone, I was still wowed by the launch video and remained incredibly impressed when I got some hands-on time with one.
Many couldn’t resist buying one despite the price – but The Verge notes that not everyone has ending up keeping the device. Apple allows you to return any product within 14 days for a full refund without having to give any reason. That window has come to an end for some of the first buyers and the site’s Alison Johnson spoke with some of those who’d decided to take advantage of it.
The iPhone Duo replaced both my iPhone 15 Pro Max and my iPad Mini 6. It now is my phone and iPad mini in my pocket. This is the dream phone I never knew I wanted.
And for the lack of Face ID, Touch ID works perfect with my Apple Watch. And even without wearing it, I don’t see the big deal of the ‘huge’ effort of bringing my finger to a button.
For the lacking 5x zoom that I had on my Pro Max, I haven’t had a moment yet that I wanted to use it to be honest. Those moments will definitely arise, but the lack of that camera cannot go up against the amazing overall experience of the iPhone Duo.
There were a few specific issues:
But the more fundamental reason for some is that it hasn’t really lived up to their hopes for a multifunctional device.
“If I can have an iPad in my pocket, that would be great.” So thought Ben Seligson, a content creator, photographer, and now former iPhone Duo owner […] “Usually I’d throw a YouTube video on the iPad or throw a podcast up. And then I start cooking dinner and leave my iPad in one spot, but I’d have my phone in my pocket if I got a text, or I needed to set a timer or something like that.” With the Duo, the phone was also the iPad on the counter, so a quick reply became much more of an interruption.
I’m curious as to whether this is just a small minority of buyers or a more common phenomenon. If you bought a Duo early enough to have hit the end of the return window, please take our poll to let us know whether you decided to keep it or return it – and do share your reasons in the comments (which are now back).
Oh, and the good news for anyone buying one now is that you’ll have a lot longer to make up your mind, with the extended return window for the holidays in place. You can now return anything bought today through January 8.

articles.title_orig: Thousands of hoax bomb alerts sent to schools in Italy, U.K. and Ireland
articles.title_zh: Thousands of hoax bomb alerts sent to schools in Italy, U.K. and Ireland
articles.content_orig:
Schools across Italy were evacuated on Wednesday ⁠after around 6,300 of them received bomb warnings, the latest in a series of threats and cyberattacks around Europe against supermarkets , blood banks, air traffic and broadcasters.
Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland said many of their schools received a similar email threat from abroad but it was classed as a hoax and did not disrupt classes.
In Italy, schools closed swiftly after ⁠the warnings, prompting many parents to drop what they were ​doing ⁠to collect children.
“My daughter Dafne started crying because the kids did not understand what was happening, and she was still shaken when I picked her up,” said Nensi Bego, parent of a child ⁠at the Mazzini middle school in Rome.
“This is so annoying. It’s obvious it’s just a hoax that disrupts ​lessons and ⁠disrupts everyone’s day.”
A copy of the ‌message seen by Reuters also included a threat to target Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni . She said the bomb alerts posed no danger and that police and other public bodies were monitoring the situation.
“All students have been taken ‌to a safe area and remain under the supervision of teaching ‌staff,” one school in Rome informed parents through a messaging app.
The email received in Italy was signed “Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan,” according to a copy of the message seen by Reuters.
“The (school) emails are public. (Sending the bomb alert messages) was as easy as drinking a ⁠glass of water,” a national security source told Reuters.
The same purported author claimed responsibility for email bomb threats sent on Friday to newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria.
Some European officials suspect Russia may be behind a campaign of disruption to everyday life in European nations supporting Ukraine after Moscow’s invasion.
Russia denies that and accuses the West of a smear campaign.
Iran is another suspect. France summoned Iran’s ambassador on Tuesday after accusing Tehran of a cyberattack that disabled refrigerators in hundreds of supermarkets last week.
Iran rejected those accusations as “baseless and hostile”.
Italian ‌Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said Wednesday’s threats were part of a clear strategy “to spread fear and ​create anxiety,” according to Adnkronos news agency.
“It is not always the work of foreign countries ‌or hostile entities. There are also attention-seekers and lunatics ⁠who, at a time like this, cannot wait to unleash terror in a city or a region,” ⁠he added.
Antonello Giannelli, head of the Italian School Principals Association, said the alerts were upsetting for students, families and school staff.
“Even though today’s ‌threats are clearly hoaxes, we cannot underestimate ​the consequences of incidents that alarm entire school communities ‌and disrupt the normal conduct of educational activities,” he ​said.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s Oregon story: Playing ping pong in Portland and waiting tables at Denny’s
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s Oregon story: Playing ping pong in Portland and waiting tables at Denny’s
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock has been one of the major winners of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. This is because the tech giant has built an AI empire, offering the world's fastest AI chips, known as graphics processing units (GPUs), and a full portfolio of supporting products and services. AI customers have snapped up Nvidia's chips, with demand often exceeding supply as the company launches new updates.
All of this has fueled mind-boggling earnings growth, with revenue and profit rising in the double and triple digits. Investors recognized this early in the AI boom, and this helped the stock soar 1,100% from the start of 2023 through the end of last year. This year has been a rockier one for Nvidia and other AI powerhouses as investors turned more cautious on the space. They worried about higher inflation in the U.S. and questioned whether data center spending would continue at current levels.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
And just this week, particularly bad news concerning Nvidia emerged. Nvidia opened an investigation into chief Jensen Huang's relationship with a person U.S. intelligence agencies are calling a Chinese spy. Against this backdrop, is Nvidia a bad-news buy or a stock to avoid? Let's find out.
Image source: Getty Images.
First, let's take a step back and consider Huang's role at Nvidia . He founded the company more than 30 years ago, and over time, he has been at the helm, guiding its direction. Huang made a major bet on AI about a decade ago, deciding to shift Nvidia's GPU focus to serving that market. Clearly, it was a winning decision. And since that time, he has become the face of AI development, speaking around the globe about the technology today and its future potential.
Huang also has lobbied to bring Nvidia's chips back to China after a U.S. export ban. He won that battle, with the U.S. permitting the export of certain chips, but China hasn't yet fully accepted imports. Nvidia has only exported a small number of chips there this year. But this situation brought the U.S./China AI race to the forefront.
All of this demonstrates something big: Huang is the driving force at Nvidia, a leader whose name is known around the world and well beyond tech circles. That suggests trouble for him could equal trouble for the company.
Now, let's consider the latest news. Nvidia on Nov. 8 said it is launching "an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Huang, in an email to staff obtained by CNBC, said that he is "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security."
The company also said in a statement to CNBC that Huang is committed to leading Nvidia "without interruption."
Nvidia's stock declined 4.2% in the following trading session, leaving the stock trading at 19x forward earnings estimates -- a level that's dirt cheap considering the company's track record of growth throughout the AI boom and prospects down the road.
Still, the current investigation introduces an element of uncertainty. So you may be wondering if you should pick up shares of Nvidia after this recent bad news or if you should avoid the stock.
The major risk the company faces is the possibility that Huang could step down or be forced out. Since he is a visionary who has driven the company for decades, and Nvidia hasn't set out a succession plan, investors could frown on such a scenario -- and that could weigh on stock performance. Another risk is that lawmakers might favor more limits regarding chip exports to China or increased regulation, moves that may weigh on future growth.
The decision to buy or avoid Nvidia right now depends on your comfort with risk. If you're a cautious investor, you might favor waiting for the results of the investigation before getting in on the stock. Though Huang intends to remain at the helm and the board has expressed confidence in him, uncertainty will linger until the investigation is complete. And this could hurt the stock in the near term. Any possible departure by Huang would also be bad news.
That said, the current turmoil doesn't change the demand present in the AI market or the quality of Nvidia's chips and innovation. Aggressive investors with a well-diversified portfolio might consider picking up a few shares of Nvidia at today's dirt cheap levels and holding on as the storm passes.

articles.title_orig: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
articles.title_zh: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
articles.content_orig:
A criminal court in Cairo has postponed the retrial of the prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, whose case has drawn international condemnation.
Wednesday's opening hearing was adjourned until 18 November after defence lawyers representing the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr requested a new judge.
The UN has warned of "widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists".
Attalah told the BBC that a recent crackdown was meant to "send a chilling message" to "the very few newsrooms that are left".
She warned: "Everybody should be careful, everybody should be scared, everybody should be wondering if they are next."
Set up 13 years ago, Mada Masr became Egypt's leading independent news site with Attalah as its editor-in-chief and co-founder.
Last month, the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court convicted her of running a website without a licence - which she said she had tried in vain for years to obtain. She was issued a hefty fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds ($56,000; £42,000) and Mada Masr was ordered to shut down.
After that trial, Attalah found that a court had previously given her a one-year prison sentence, without her knowledge, for "spreading false news" - a charge often used against journalists and dissidents - as well as operating a website without a licence. It was issued in absentia in 2024, even though she was in the country at the time. Attalah is now being retried in that case by the same judge.
At the opening session, Attalah's defence team requested the judge's recusal, arguing that he had "already formed a conviction in mind against the defendant", Mada Masr cited its lawyer Hassan al-Azhar as saying . The judge went into recess before adjourning proceedings for a week to allow the court to consider the defence's request, he added.
Mada Masr also said Attalah's appeal against last month's conviction was scheduled to take place on 25 November.
Egypt has largely stifled freedom of the press, ranking 169th out of 180 countries for press freedom, according to Reporters Without Borders' 2026 analysis. The group says that at least 26 journalists who were arrested in recent years remain in detention.
While most newspapers and television stations now keep to government lines, Mada Masr remained a rare, independent and investigative news source in Egypt. However, since 2017 the site could only be viewed from outside the country.
It had reported on alleged corruption and human rights abuses, and provided deep coverage of politics and economics, as well as regional upheaval and wars in Libya, Sudan and Gaza.
In her BBC interview on Sunday, Attalah insisted that the factual reporting and professional standards of Mada Masr had an important role to play in Egyptian society, which could benefit the government.
"It's much better if you have a little space left to have it open for professional media organisations who do rigorous reporting, because if we disappear, then you make the space for conspiracies and disinformation," she said.
"People need to know, people need to consume information and you're shooting yourself in the foot if you're killing the newsrooms that do it properly."
In September, six journalists with the independent fact-checking platform, Matsda2sh - constituting its entire newsroom - were arrested in home raids by the Egyptian authorities and held incommunicado for nearly a week.
They have since been charged with joining the Muslim Brotherhood and financing terrorism, and their lawyers report that several were beaten and electrocuted in detention. They say that no evidence has been presented linking them to the Brotherhood.
Egypt's former president Mohammed Morsi – who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood – was removed from power by the military, led by Abdul Fattah al-Sisi, in July 2013 after widespread protests. Under Sisi, who became president the following year, the Islamist movement was classed as a terrorist organisation, leading to a widespread clampdown.
On Tuesday, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Thameen Al-Kheetan, called for the Matsda2sh reporters to be released, with all charges dropped.
He also said the case against Attalah "raises fresh concerns regarding due process and fair trial".
"We call on Egypt to end all forms of harassment of journalists and media outlets, and to respect and fulfil the right to freedom of expression, including the right to information," Al-Kheetan said.
"The steps taken to suppress the continued work of both Matsda2sh and Mada Masr must be overturned. The people of Egypt have a right to read and hear views expressed through these fora on issues of legitimate public concern."
Attalah has suggested the authorities might again be trying to silence independent voices at a time of economic strain in Egypt and regional instability.
It has been widely noted that recent legal action against journalists comes after the US State Department waived human rights conditions on $320m (£240m) in its foreign military funding for Egypt in September. This allowed the funds to be released as part of Washington's annual $1.3bn military aid package.
The BBC asked US Secretary of State Marco Rubio whether he had raised the recent crackdown on independent journalism with Egypt's Foreign Minister, Badr Abdelatty, at their meeting about regional tensions in Paris on Monday.
"We didn't discuss it today," Rubio said. "But… like anything else in foreign policy, there's always a balancing act to further the national interest of the United States. And in the end, Egypt has been a reliable and good defence partner of the United States."
"That doesn't mean you agree with everything another government does," he went on, adding that he was not "opining about their journalists".

articles.title_orig: Four bears killed in Canada after attack on mother and daughter
articles.title_zh: Four bears killed in Canada after attack on mother and daughter
articles.content_orig:
Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in British Columbia (file image)
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.
Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.
"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.
"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

articles.title_orig: Fed's Goolsbee calls inflation report 'borderline disturbing' as central bank weighs more hikes
articles.title_zh: Fed's Goolsbee calls inflation report 'borderline disturbing' as central bank weighs more hikes
articles.content_orig:
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest inflation data "borderline disturbing."
"It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said in an interview with "PBS NewsHour " on Tuesday.
"We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Goolsbee said. "We're going to have to deal with that."
The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Tuesday morning release. That was higher than economists had predicted, and the third straight month of outsized price increases.
Goolsbee said he had not seen drivers of prices like tariffs fade over time like he had hoped. He also said continuously high inflation on services concerned him.
And the Chicago Fed chief said lofty prices are a top issue for many people he meets.
"It's on everyone's mind," Goolsbee said. "It's on business mind. It's on nonprofits' minds. It's on ordinary consumers' mind."
Tuesday's inflation report landed at a critical juncture for the central bankers at the Federal Reserve as they considers their next interest rate move — and the moves they may have to make in the months ahead if the numbers continue to come in hot.
Goolsbee's comments arrived on the heels of remarks from other Fed officials Tuesday who said the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee may need to act more decisively to rein in inflation.
When it raises or lowers rates, the Fed typically moves by a quarter-percentage point. But Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in London early Tuesday that a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for an outsized half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if the core CPI, a metric that removes volatile food and energy costs, was "around 0.3." Hours later, that's exactly what happened.
Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking Tuesday after the inflation report, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases, and said "it may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall."
Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed, was more sanguine. While she acknowledged that "inflation pressures are still very much with us," she said Tuesday that the central bank didn't need to move too quickly. "For now, further gradual tightening seems appropriate," she said. "The exact path will depend on how conditions evolve, and I'll be watching the data closely."
The committee raised rates by a quarter point in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%, before voting to hold them steady in October.
After years of higher-than-preferred price growth , Goolsbee said the possibility of consumers and businesses beginning to expect hot inflation is a "major concern." If that does happen, he said it can make the process of cooling inflation "much more painful."
But Goolsbee didn't specify whether he thought the Fed should hike rates at its December policy gathering as a result of these concerns. "I'm not a fan of being very specific and tying our hands at the next meeting or meetings in the future," Goolsbee said.
Waller, Logan and Paulson are voting members of the FOMC this year, which means they will cast votes on whether to raise rates at the committee's final meeting of the year in December. Goolsbee will be a voting member next year.
In the wake of the inflation report and the remarks from the various Fed officials, fed funds futures are now unanimously expecting a rate hike at the December meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
Now the question is about whether the central bank will raise rates by a quarter or half percentage point. The fed funds futures currently put the odds of a half-point hike at the upcoming December meeting at 15%.
Odds of rates reaching 4.25%-4.5% by the January meeting — the equivalent of either a single half-point rise or two quarter-point hikes — are now at 60%, with a 10% chance of rates hitting 4.5%-4.75% by then.

articles.title_orig: Sneaky fee on airport purchase sparks outrage after traveler shares receipt: 'Out of control'
articles.title_zh: Sneaky fee on airport purchase sparks outrage after traveler shares receipt: 'Out of control'
articles.content_orig:
A traveler buying a $21.99 book at a self checkout in Hudson’s Bryant Park Market in JFK Airport Terminal 5 was charged a mandatory 3% “employee retention” surcharge, with sales tax added on top of the fee, View from the Wing reported on November 5, citing the passenger’s receipt. Port Authority rules allow airport concessions to add an employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3% of the pre-tax bill, according to its street pricing regulation .
For travelers passing through JFK, LaGuardia or Newark, the rule means a small percentage can be added to shop and restaurant bills on top of shelf prices. It is a fee, not a tip, and it applies whether the purchase is made at a counter or a machine. Our guide to the closest airport to New York City compares the three airports.
The receipt showed a 3% surcharge described as being for employee and retention programs and “not a gratuity,” View from the Wing said. Sales tax was charged on the surcharge as well as on the book. The passenger shared the receipt on Reddit, the outlet said, and it did not report any response from the Port Authority or the retailer.
On a $21.99 purchase, a 3% fee adds about 66 cents before tax. The amount is small on a single item, but it applies across a bill, so a family buying meals and snacks before a long flight would pay the fee on the whole total.
The Port Authority’s street pricing rule, in effect since January 1, 2025, says airport concessions may not charge more than 115% of street prices, the regular prices for similar goods in the New York and New Jersey metro area. The same rule lets them add an employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3% of the pre-tax total on a bill, and that fee does not count as a violation of the cap.
The regulation says the fee covers particular costs of doing business at the airport compared with locations outside it. Terminal operators or the Port Authority can issue violation notices after price reviews, which may include spot checks, and concessions then have 48 hours to fix prices, according to the document.
View from the Wing said similar fees have appeared at Newark, which is also a Port Authority airport, and at Philadelphia. It also cited a 4.5% hospitality charge at Minneapolis restaurants and tipping prompts at an Austin airport shop. Fees like these vary by airport and by business, so the total at checkout can differ from the price on the shelf or the menu, even for the same item.
Travelers who want to keep costs down can pack snacks and an empty water bottle to fill after security, and check the receipt or payment screen before paying. Buying books, chargers and other items before reaching the airport avoids both higher airport prices and the fee. For another way to trim airport costs, see our story on changes to Lyft airport ride discounts .
Travelers who think they were charged more than the rules allow can keep the receipt and raise it with the terminal’s customer service desk. The regulation sets out enforcement through terminal operators and the Port Authority, though it does not describe a public complaint process.
The fee in this case appeared at a self checkout, where no employee served the customer, which is what drew attention online, View from the Wing said. The Port Authority rule ties the fee to employee wage and benefit costs at the airport overall, not to whether a worker handles a given sale. That is why it can appear on purchases at a machine.
66 cents. Fee on a $21.99 book.
Yes, up to 3% of the pre-tax total.
No. The receipt said it is not a gratuity.
It was in the JFK case reported.
Up to 115% of street prices, plus the fee.

articles.title_orig: Russian diplomat says Moscow could conclude non-aggression pacts with NATO member states
articles.title_zh: Russian diplomat says Moscow could conclude non-aggression pacts with NATO member states
articles.content_orig:
Alexei Drobinin, Head of the Foreign Policy Planning Department at the Russian Foreign Ministry, has set out Russia's ideas for a new European security framework, saying that Moscow and NATO member states could sign non-aggression agreements.
Source: European Pravda, citing Reuters
Details: Vladimir Medinsky, Russia's chief negotiator at the talks on Ukraine, which resumed this week for the first time since February, stated on Wednesday that a new European security system had been the central topic of the two-day negotiations in Abu Dhabi. However, he did not specify what exactly the meeting participants had discussed.
Drobinin outlined several detailed proposals for the new security system at a conference in Moscow on Wednesday.
The first option would be to establish a collective defence alliance or sign bilateral mutual assistance agreements, similar to Russia's agreements with Belarus and North Korea.
The second would involve political agreements committing each side not to support the other's adversaries in the event of aggression, similar to Moscow's pact with Iran.
The third would be bilateral non-aggression pacts.
Quote from Drobinin: "For example, agreements of this kind could be reached, among other things, with individual NATO member states, which would then receive, for instance, additional individual security guarantees from the Russian Federation."
Details: Some European politicians oppose any discussions on the overall European security architecture, emphasising that agreements on progress in resolving the war in Ukraine, including a ceasefire, must be reached first. Meanwhile, US officials have made it clear that they are open to such discussions.

articles.title_orig: Kenya's Ebola outbreak: Last patient discharged as countdown begins to be being declared free of the virus
articles.title_zh: Kenya's Ebola outbreak: Last patient discharged as countdown begins to be being declared free of the virus
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free.
It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died.
Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation.
"Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak.
"This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X.
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October.
All the Kenyan cases were linked to the man who had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda, with health officials reporting no evidence of wider community transmission.
Those who have recovered following treatment included four healthcare workers.
Five patients were discharged on 3 November, followed by a sixth three days later, before the final patient was cleared on Wednesday.
Under World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, 42 days must pass after the last patient tests negative and is discharged, or the last Ebola victim is safely buried, before an outbreak can be declared over.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Duale said the government would maintain heightened surveillance at border crossings, airports, health facilities and communities throughout the countdown.
Emergency response teams will remain on alert across the country, while the health authorities will continue monitoring travellers arriving from affected countries.
Kenyans returning from Ebola-affected areas are required to complete electronic health declarations before travelling, undergo screening on arrival and spend 21 days in quarantine under the supervision of health teams.
The minister also urged countries that had imposed travel and visa restrictions to reconsider them - adding that Kenya had no intention of serving as a quarantine centre for another country.
In May, a Kenyan court suspended US plans to open an Ebola quarantine facility for American citizens.
Kenya has maintained that there is no need to restrict domestic travel, trade or public gatherings.
The outbreak has nevertheless disrupted international travel, with some Gulf countries introducing restrictions affecting travellers from Kenya and other African countries.
Saudi Arabia stopped issuing visas to Kenyan nationals in late October, prompting concerns among those seeking employment there.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has announced that it is lifting its suspension on issuing new visas to Ugandan nationals, easing restrictions introduced in June.
But Ugandans will have to spend at least 21 days outside of Uganda before being allowed to travel to the UAE.
The UAE is also allowing certain students, diplomatic passport holders and Ugandan embassy employees to enter under approved health procedures.
Uganda, which shares a long and busy border with DR Congo, was among the countries first affected but declared its own Ebola outbreak over on 27 August.
The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

articles.title_orig: John Kerry: America Must Now Follow China’s Lead on Clean Energy
articles.title_zh: John Kerry: America Must Now Follow China’s Lead on Clean Energy
articles.content_orig:
Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’
Cop31 live – latest updates
China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels , and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.
Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.
“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”
For autocratic states without free and fair elections , seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added.
“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”
He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”
China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.
Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way : “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”
The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows .
Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.
The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue.
after newsletter promotion
“Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”
Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed .
Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.
China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.
Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”
If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.
Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.
They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.
For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … so no major drama.”

articles.title_orig: US to seek Putin’s ‘blessing’ for Europe to join Ukraine talks
articles.title_zh: US to seek Putin’s ‘blessing’ for Europe to join Ukraine talks
articles.content_orig:
ABU DHABI — U.S. officials will head to Moscow in person Thursday to ask Russian President Vladimir Putin to give his “blessing” to allow European representatives to join future peace talks for Ukraine.
Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law who has been mediating talks in Abu Dhabi, told reporters he and White House envoy Steve Witkoff will head to Moscow to meet the Russian leader.
They aim to secure Putin’s approval for Europe to get a seat at the table and to sign off on what would be the biggest prisoner exchange since the start of the war. Kushner said European participation is critical for discussions over revising the future security architecture of Europe — a longstanding Russian demand, and an initiative that has alarmed some European officials.
“We need to have the Europeans at the table,” Kushner told POLITICO. “We have relayed to President Putin directly several times and to his team that the only way to get this done is to have them by our side and I think they are receptive to it.
“I believe that hopefully tomorrow in Moscow, Steve and I will be successful and President Putin will give the blessing for that to occur. I think that if he agrees to that we will be able to make a lot more progress on the issues that matter.”
The talks in Abu Dhabi are the first between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. since February. Ukraine and its allies in Europe had played down expectations of a breakthrough at the talks, and no progress was announced on critical issues such as ceasefires on energy infrastructure, Black Sea shipping or territory.
But the fact the sides were meeting again after nine months without any discussions was seen in European capitals as an important step.
In one move designed to build confidence between the warring nations, Kushner announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to what is likely to be “the biggest” exchange of prisoners since the start of the war. The numbers will be confirmed Thursday, he added. Russian state-controlled news agency Tass confirmed that a “large-scale” prisoner exchange had been agreed.
Kushner said that, overall, the two-day talk were “substantive” and “pretty tough” but “a good first step” to get the two sides talking again after a nine-month break.
He said that when U.S. officials met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo three weeks ago, it was not clear that Moscow and Kyiv would be able to resume negotiations.
“It’s been a long way to get everyone back to the table,” Kushner said. “But I think this was a very good first meeting. It was a tough meeting, but a productive one.” He said all relevant issues were discussed between the two sides and that the question of territory “will be the hardest” to resolve.
The Ukrainian negotiators blamed “very strict directives” from the Kremlin for limiting their room to negotiate in Abu Dhabi, making it impossible to make more progress in the talks.
Kushner and Witkoff will aim to persuade Putin to unlock progress on some issues in their meeting with him Thursday and, according to officials who took part in the talks, to agree the date of the next round of negotiations. They will then travel to meet Zelenskyy and potentially European leaders in Dublin on Friday.
Ukraine wants an agreement on a ceasefire by the New Year, as it fears Russia is preparing another winter of bombardments and targeting energy networks to freeze the country into submission.
One critical question, especially for Europe, is how far the talks about changing the continental security framework underpinned by NATO will be tied to the specific negotiations over peace in Ukraine.
Europeans have long campaigned for Ukraine to get the strongest possible security guarantees to prevent Russia attacking again when this war ends. U.S. officials want to explore the idea of providing a NATO-like collective defense agreement with Ukraine which could even see the alliance itself as a guarantor.
But Russia is insisting on widening the talks to include a review of the whole security architecture for Europe — something the U.S. mediators have agreed.
European officials say the sequencing of these talks will be critical. The European side has signaled its willingness to explore overhauling the continent’s wider security system to allay Russia’s concerns — in parallel with the Ukraine peace process. But they do not want to sign up to any broader reforms until peace has been achieved.
Kushner said the aim was to discuss all the issues and then “find a pathway to settle them all at the same time.”
“I think that having these discussions is very important,” he said. “But the implementation of postwar security will not occur until there’s an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues.”
The U.S. desire to have Europe join the negotiations throws the spotlight back on the European Union and others such as the United Kingdom to decide who will represent them in talks. EU leaders will consider this now urgent question in Dublin at an informal summit Friday.
Zelenskyy has said he wants to be consulted over who gets to represent Europe, but has urged his allies to hurry up and ideally pick one person to take the lead in future talks .
Kushner said the current arrangement, which includes NATO, the EU institutions, and representatives from France, Germany, the U.K and Italy, was “a really strong way to organize,” adding, “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.”

articles.title_orig: 400 Mawozo: Headquarters of Haitian gang destroyed, El Salvador's president says
articles.title_zh: 400 Mawozo: Headquarters of Haitian gang destroyed, El Salvador's president says
articles.content_orig:
El Salvador's president posted a video on X of the strikes on a complex he said is the headquarters of 400 Mawozo
Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-AimÃ© has praised "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs" after a joint strike on a house allegedly used by the leader of the 400 Mawozo gang.
El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele, had earlier announced that a joint task force had "destroyed" what he described as "the house of LanmÃ² San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters".
A small contingent of Salvadorean troops has been in Haiti since January 2025 as part of a multinational force deployed to suppress gang violence.
Last month, Bukele sent an extra 2,000 soldiers to rescue four Salvadoreans who have been missing since they were ambushed on 18 October.
Bukele's post on X , external was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex.
As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.
Writing in Creole, Bukele said "we kept our promise", adding that the alleged gang members "ran away without even trying to fight".
Local media reported that as many as 20 people were killed in the strike, which they said was carried out in the early hours of Sunday.
They also reported that LanmÃ² San Jou, whose real name is Wilson Joseph, was not at the property at the time of the attack.
Posting on X on Tuesday, Fils-AimÃ© thanked the Salvadorean military's commitment "in the fight against gangs" and said the two nations would keep working together, along with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority".
"THE GANGS WILL GET NO SLEEP!" he added.
While he did not provide any further details about the joint operation or the number of casualties, Fils-AimÃ© posted a still from the video shared by Bukele showing a helicopter firing a projectile at the compound.
The BBC has not been able to verify the video posted by Bukele, nor whether the property is indeed the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo, Haiti's largest criminal gang, which is infamous for carrying out kidnappings for ransom.
Salvadorean troops have become a regular sight in Port-au-Prince
The attack on the alleged gang headquarters seemingly came after a user on X had urged Bukele to attack the complex.
"Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we'll destroy it," the Salvadorean president replied to the post, which has now been taken down, apparently for violating X's rules.
Bukele has threatened Haitian gangs before.
Following the kidnapping of four Salvadorean air force technicians on 18 October, he addressed "the gang leaders and gang members holding our four compatriots hostage in Haiti" directly.
"We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too," he wrote in Creole, referring to his crackdown on gang violence in his own country.
The four abducted Salvadoreans were working as part of the GSF, made up of troops from several nations.
Bukele's decision to send thousands of additional troops to Haiti since their abduction has raised concerns with critics who say they are not all working within the command structure of the GSF.
It has also raised questions about the operational legitimacy and legality of their actions in the Caribbean nation.
Amnesty International has urged both countries to "ensure all operations conducted by Salvadorean forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law".

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock extended its decline Tuesday, falling roughly 5% after dropping 4% in the prior session. The stock came under pressure amid a broader market sell-off and growing concerns about increased scrutiny of the chipmaker following CEO Jensen Huang's admission to an affair believed to involve a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Scrutiny centers on Alice Huang, whom the US government reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset, and her ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dating back to at least 2023.
The Information reported that their rapport could have helped facilitate the shipment of at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Chinese companies, according to two people who know her and corporate records.
On Monday, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Congress needs more answers about the matter, adding that there are "real ⁠concerns that need to be addressed with respect to the ​Nvidia situation."
President Trump, meanwhile, told reporters that the FBI was looking into Huang's relationship, while still expressing support for the Nvidia CEO.
"We'll look into it," said Trump. "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape."
The broader semiconductor sector wavered on Tuesday amid a broader market sell-off after a hotter-than-expected October inflation reading, which strengthened expectations for a rate hike next month.
Rrival AMD ( AMD ) stock rose 4% before giving up gains. Broadcom ( AVGO ) shares gained more than 1%, while Intel ( INTC ) stock was little changed.
Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company ( TSM ), which manufactures Nvidia chips, wavered, while semiconductor equipment maker ASML ( ASML ) slipped into red territory.
Storage maker Sandisk ( SNDK ) and memory chipmakers Micron Technology ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) declined.

articles.title_orig: Reform boycotts Senedd after member banned for saying white people being replaced
articles.title_zh: Reform boycotts Senedd after member banned for saying white people being replaced
articles.content_orig:
Reform UK will partially boycott the Senedd to protest the ban of one of their politicians for claiming white people are being "replaced".
The party's Welsh leader, Helen Jenner, said Joe Martin's ban was because of "undue pressure" from governing party Plaid Cymru and was an "infringement on freedom of speech".
Martin had been told he would not be allowed to speak in the Senedd's chamber until he apologised for the remarks, which the parliament's Presiding Officer Huw Irranca-Davies called "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called the ruling "ridiculous and outrageous".
Reform, which is by far the Senedd's largest opposition party, said its members would withdraw from most of Wednesday's proceedings before returning to vote in the parliament later in the evening.
Jenner confirmed her party's boycott on the steps of the Senedd on Wednesday afternoon.
"It is now clear that the freedom of speech of one of our Senedd members is being curtailed, meaning his constituents are being silenced," she said.
"We stand behind Joe, and we will not attend today's plenary session in protest at his treatment.
"Every Reform MS [Member of the Senedd] will be in their Senedd office working hard for our constituents."
Martin said he would not apologise.
"My voters sent me to the Senedd to speak on their behalf," he said.
"I am being blocked from doing so, and now it's clear that I have fewer rights than the people who elected me. That cannot be the situation in a national parliament."
Asked by BBC Wales if he genuinely believed white people were being "replaced" in the UK, Martin said: "That's obviously a fact."
Posting on X, Farage said it was "ridiculous and outrageous that Reform's duly elected Member of the Senedd, Joe Martin, has been banned from speaking in the Welsh Parliament".
"Why is it only Reform that's targeted like this?" he asked.
Martin was also backed by the leader of right-wing party Restore Britain, Rupert Lowe.
He called for the Senedd to be "shut down" if it was "going to shut down legitimate debate around demographic security and immigration".
Martin's Caerdydd Penarth constituency includes some of Wales' most ethnically diverse communities.
On Tuesday Martin asked for a Welsh government statement on the "demographic replacement of white British people" during business questions, when Senedd members are free to raise issues they choose.
Business Minister Heledd Fychan immediately asked the presiding officer whether the remarks were within the Senedd's standing orders - a set of rules that govern conduct in the chamber.
Standing orders give the presiding officer discretion to decide if contributions to plenary sessions - meetings of the full Senedd - use "discriminatory or offensive language".
Delivering his ruling later, Irranca-Davies said: "Until I receive a clear indication that the member understands the boundaries of acceptable parliamentary conduct and apologises to the Siambr [chamber], we will not be calling him to speak."
Senedd officials confirmed an apology would have to be made in the chamber during a plenary session.
The ruling does not cover committees.
Martin is a member of the Senedd's Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee.
Irranca-Davies pointed out it was not the first time he has rebuked Martin. In September, he said Martin had made offensive remarks about surgeons working in the Welsh NHS gender service .
Plaid Cymru Senedd member Carrie Harper called Reform's boycott a "pathetic tantrum" that was a "disgrace to democracy".
"They'd rather play gimmicks and chase headlines than be serious about Wales' future and doing the job they were elected to do on behalf of the people they represent," she said.
In the 2021 census 93.8% of people in Wales identified as white, down from 95.6% a decade earlier, with the country's overall population growing by 1.4% to 3,107,500.
The proportion identifying as Asian, Asian Welsh or Asian British, the next highest group in the survey, rose from 2.3% to 2.9%.
Mixed or multiple ethnic groups rose from 1% to 1.6%, and those identifying as Black, Black Welsh, Black British, Caribbean or African rose from 0.6% to 0.9%.
